Quantum Interfaces: transferring quantum information between light and matter

Lecture 2: The platforms, the links and what limits them

Shayne Bennetts

IAMS Yb Lab, Institute of Atomic and Molecular Sciences, Academia Sinica

TIGP, Tuesday 24 November 2026

2.5

Linking nodes: the repeater problem and heralded entanglement

Fibre loss · the repeater · memories · atom-photon entanglement · Hong-Ou-Mandel · teleportation · one click or two · linked atomic clouds · spin echo · link rate · distillation · frequency conversion

2.5

The numbers of lecture 1 decide how well a link works

  • Nodes A and B, L apart, send photons to a beam splitter with two detectors
  • C1 or β says how well each node couples to its mode
  • η is the fraction of photons collected, transmitted and detected
  • The rate of pairs is the probability per attempt times the attempt rate
  • ηlink=γent/γdec is the rate of pairs over the rate at which the memories lose them
Covey, Weinfurter and Bernien, npj Quantum Inf. 9, 90 (2023), arXiv:2304.02088
2.5-1

The symbols are those of lecture 1, unchanged

SymbolMeaning
ΓNatural linewidth, the population decay rate, Γ=1/τ
γ=Γ/2Decay rate of the dipole amplitude
Ω, ΔFull Rabi frequency; detuning Δ=ωL−ω0
gSingle-photon coupling; the vacuum Rabi splitting is 2g
κCavity field decay rate, the half width
C1=g2/(2κγ)Single-atom cooperativity
β=Γ1D/(Γ1D+Γ′)Fraction into the guided mode; β=2C1/(1+2C1)
OD=−lnTOptical depth on resonance; OD≈2Nβ on a waveguide
  • Widths are quoted as Γ/2π; a paper's own value and form follow in brackets
Reiserer and Rempe, Rev. Mod. Phys. 87, 1379 (2015), arXiv:1412.2889, Eqs. 2 and 4
2.5-2

A photon's survival in fibre falls exponentially with length

T=e−L/Latt=10−αL/10
  • Latt is the attenuation length; α is the loss in dB/km
  • At 854 nm, about 3 dB/km, a photon survives 50 km with probability 10−15
  • At 1550 nm the loss is 0.181 dB/km, but the fall is still exponential
  • The rate of a direct link falls the same way
  • Made in segments L0 and then joined (dashed), it falls only as a power: (L0/L)2
Krutyanskiy et al., npj Quantum Inf. 5, 72 (2019), arXiv:1901.06317; Duan et al., Nature 414, 413 (2001), arXiv:quant-ph/0105105, p. 5
2.5-3

Entanglement swapping joins two pairs into one

  • A Bell measurement on b and c leaves A and D entangled, though they never met
  • Two classical bits tell D which of four corrections to apply
Żukowski et al., Phys. Rev. Lett. 71, 4287 (1993); Hermans et al., Nature 605, 663 (2022), arXiv:2110.11373
2.5-4

A repeater joins short entangled links into one long one

  • Each segment of length L0, about one Latt, is entangled on its own and kept until needed
  • A Bell measurement at an orange node swaps two pairs into one twice as long
  • Purification makes one better pair from two noisy ones, as distillation shows later
  • Purifying and swapping in turn, the resources grow only polynomially with distance
  • Local errors at the percent level are tolerated
Briegel, Dür, Cirac and Zoller, Phys. Rev. Lett. 81, 5932 (1998), arXiv:quant-ph/9803056; Żukowski et al., Phys. Rev. Lett. 71, 4287 (1993)
2.5-5

A memory turns a chance of p² per attempt into about p

⟨N⟩a=1p2,⟨N⟩b=3−2pp(2−p)≈32p
  • Each of two segments heralds a pair (orange dot) with probability p per attempt
  • ⟨N⟩ is the mean number of attempts until both hold a pair
  • a: without memories, both must succeed in the same attempt
  • b: a memory keeps the first pair (blue bar) until the second arrives
  • Two ions, 25 km to each side: 7.2×10−6 per attempt without memory, 9.2×10−4 with it
Krutyanskiy et al., Phys. Rev. Lett. 130, 213601 (2023), arXiv:2210.05418, p. 3 and Supplemental Material, Eq. S4
2.5-6

A satellite avoids the exponential loss of fibre

  • One photon of each pair goes down to each of two stations 1203 km apart
  • The two downlinks, 1600 to 2400 km together, lose 64 to 82 dB (orange box)
  • Against 1200 km of fibre (blue line), the link gains 12 to 17 orders of magnitude
  • 5.9×106 pairs per second at the source, about 1.1 per second reach both stations
  • Post-selected F≥0.87±0.09; CHSH S=2.37±0.09, above the classical bound 2
Yin et al., Science 356, 1140 (2017), arXiv:1707.01339, Fig. 4
2.5-7

A decaying atom leaves its qubit entangled with its photon

|Ψ⟩AP=(|↓⟩|L⟩+|↑⟩|R⟩)/2
  • A 87Rb atom in mF=0 is excited to |e⟩, which has F′=0
  • A decay to mF=−1, called |↓⟩, emits a left-circular photon |L⟩
  • A decay to mF=+1, called |↑⟩, emits a right-circular photon |R⟩
  • Nothing records which decay happened, so atom A and photon P stay in superposition
  • Colour or arrival time can carry the photon's qubit instead
Hofmann et al., Science 337, 72 (2012), Fig. 1B; Moehring et al., Nature 449, 68 (2007); Knaut et al., Nature 629, 573 (2024), arXiv:2310.01316
2.5-8

Two photons on a beam splitter herald a Bell state

  • Identical photons leave the beam splitter by the same port
  • Polarisations H and V in different outputs herald |Ψ−⟩; in the same output, |Ψ+⟩
Hong, Ou and Mandel, Phys. Rev. Lett. 59, 2044 (1987), Fig. 2; Hofmann et al., Science 337, 72 (2012)
2.5-9

A pair is judged by its fidelity to a Bell state

  • The fidelity F is the overlap of the pair's measured state ρ with the target Bell state
  • F above one half proves that the two qubits are entangled
  • Heralded means that a signal announces the pair, and the pair is kept for use
  • Post-selected means that only trials with both photons detected count, and no pair is left
  • Deterministic means that every trial delivers a pair
Hofmann et al., Science 337, 72 (2012); Krutyanskiy et al., Phys. Rev. Lett. 130, 050803 (2023), arXiv:2208.14907; van Leent et al., Nature 607, 69 (2022), arXiv:2111.15526; Covey, Weinfurter and Bernien, npj Quantum Inf. 9, 90 (2023), arXiv:2304.02088
2.5-10

Teleportation sends a qubit with a shared pair and two bits

  • Without the pair, a qubit measured and sent as numbers arrives with average fidelity at most 2/3
  • Feed-forward chooses the correction from the bits in real time, while the qubit waits
Bennett et al., Phys. Rev. Lett. 70, 1895 (1993); Riebe et al., Nature 429, 734 (2004); Hermans et al., Nature 605, 663 (2022), arXiv:2110.11373; Main et al., Nature 638, 383 (2025), arXiv:2407.00835
2.5-11

Two ways to herald: one click or two photons

  • a: each node emits with a small probability p; one click heralds a pair with F≈1−p
  • The rate goes as η; the paths must hold to a fraction of a wavelength
  • For atomic ensembles and 10 km links, the path difference must stay δx≤0.1 µm for about 30 s
  • b: a coincidence of two photons heralds |Ψ−⟩
  • The rate goes as η2; the paths need hold only to about 0.3 m
  • This path tolerance is about 3×106 times looser than in scheme a
Chen et al., Phys. Rev. A 76, 022329 (2007), arXiv:quant-ph/0609151; Moehring et al., Nature 449, 68 (2007); Krutyanskiy et al., npj Quantum Inf. 5, 72 (2019), arXiv:1901.06317
2.5-12

One click wins at low efficiency, two photons at high

H1=2P×0.1,H2=P2/2
  • H1 and H2 are the chances per attempt of a herald by one click and by two photons
  • P is the probability that one node's photon is generated, transmitted and detected
  • For one click, each node emits with p=0.1, so that F≈1−p=0.9
  • At P=0.01 and 2 kHz, one click gives 4 heralds a second, two photons 0.1
  • Above P=0.4 (calculated) the two-photon herald wins
Krutyanskiy et al., npj Quantum Inf. 5, 72 (2019), arXiv:1901.06317
2.5-13

In DLCZ, one click shares one excitation between two clouds

S†=N−1/2∑i|s⟩i⟨g|
(SL†±eiϕSR†)|0⟩L|0⟩R/2
  • a: a weak write pulse makes one excitation S† with probability pc≪1
  • b: read pulses turn I₁ and I₂ into photons; one click joins the two links
  • Loss only lengthens the wait T0~tΔ/(ηppc), for attempts of length tΔ and efficiency ηp
  • Joined efficiently, the time grows as (L/L0)2
Duan, Lukin, Cirac and Zoller, Nature 414, 413 (2001), arXiv:quant-ph/0105105, Eq. 6
2.5-14

A spin echo undoes the spread of frequencies in a memory

  • The spins fan out in T2*; a π pulse at τ reverses every phase, and they realign at 2τ
  • Dynamical decoupling repeats the π pulse; T2 is the decay that no pulse undoes
Pham et al., Phys. Rev. B 86, 045214 (2012), arXiv:1201.5686; Hermans et al., Nature 605, 663 (2022), arXiv:2110.11373; Main et al., Nature 638, 383 (2025), arXiv:2407.00835
2.5-15

The rate of pairs is compared with the decay of the memories

  • Attempts at rate f for a fraction d of the time, each heralding with P=η2/2, give R=fPd
  • ηlink=γent/γdec=RT2; above one, pairs come faster than they decay
Covey, Weinfurter and Bernien, npj Quantum Inf. 9, 90 (2023), arXiv:2304.02088; Moehring et al., Nature 449, 68 (2007); Hucul et al., Nat. Phys. 11, 37 (2015), arXiv:1403.3696; van Leent et al., Nature 607, 69 (2022), arXiv:2111.15526
2.5-16

Distillation turns many noisy pairs into fewer better ones

  • Both nodes measure the same parity checks on their halves of n pairs of error p=1−F
  • A sends its outcomes sA to B, which discards on a mismatch (heralded) or corrects (deterministic)
  • With perfect local gates, the two-pair check, repeated, purifies pairs of error below 50 %
  • With real gates, simple protocols stop at about ten times the local gate error
  • A high-rate code makes each pair of error 2×10−4 from 3.6 pairs of 5 % error (calculated)
Bonilla Ataides et al., Phys. Rev. Lett. 135, 130804 (2025), arXiv:2502.09542, Table II; Ramette et al., npj Quantum Inf. 10, 58 (2024), arXiv:2302.01296; Dür et al., Phys. Rev. A 59, 169 (1999), arXiv:quant-ph/9808065; Bennett et al., Phys. Rev. A 54, 3824 (1996), arXiv:quant-ph/9604024
2.5-17

The wavelength decides where frequency conversion pays

  • a: in a χ(2) crystal a strong 1902 nm pump turns an 854 nm photon into 1550 nm
  • The pump's Raman scattering adds noise photons
  • The fibre loses about 0.1 dB/m at 369.5 nm and 3 dB/km at 854 nm
  • b: the dashed curve is 854 nm light converted with 25 % efficiency
  • For 854 nm, conversion pays beyond the dot, near 2 km (calculated)
Moehring et al., Nature 449, 68 (2007), for 369.5 nm; Krutyanskiy et al., npj Quantum Inf. 5, 72 (2019), arXiv:1901.06317, for 854 nm, 1550 nm and the conversion
2.5-18
2.6

Trapped ions

Two ions linked through lenses · the rate budget · an ion in a cavity and what its mirrors cost · conversion to 1550 nm · heralded links from 2007 to 2025 · time bins · the choices and the limits

2.6

Two ions 1 m apart, entangled by their photons

  • Two 171Yb+ ions 1 m apart send their photons to a beam splitter; a coincidence heralds |Ψ−⟩
  • Each photon carries its ion's qubit in its frequency, ν↑ or ν↓, 12.6 GHz apart (a)
  • A path difference Δx turns each phase by kΔx (b, grey); the herald keeps only ΔkΔx (blue)
  • Δk is the photons' difference in wave number: 2π/Δk = 2.4 cm (c)
  • Heralded F=0.63±0.03, at 2.0×10−3 s−1
Moehring et al., Nature 449, 68 (2007), Fig. 1a and Methods, Eqs. 2 to 4
2.6-1

Two photons are needed, so the efficiencies enter squared

P=14[12qDζTρPexcε]2≈3.6×10−9
R=fP=2.0×10−3 s−1
  • An ion emits a 369.5 nm photon with probability ρPexc = 0.995 × 0.5
  • The lens collects ε = 0.02 of the solid angle
  • Fibre, optics, a polariser and the detector pass ζ=0.2, T=0.8, ½ and qD=0.15
  • Both photons must arrive (orange); a coincidence heralds only |Ψ−⟩ of the four Bell states
  • Attempts at f=5.5×105 s−1 give R=fP pairs a second
Moehring et al., Nature 449, 68 (2007), p. 70
2.6-2

The first ion link to make pairs faster than they decohere

ηlink=Rτm≈4.5 s−1×1.12 s≈5
  • Two 171Yb+ modules about 1 m apart share a beam splitter (a); b scales this up
  • Attempts at 470 kHz succeed with probability 9.7×10−6: R = 4.5 pairs a second
  • Heralded F=0.78±0.03, the mean of the two heralded Bell states
  • Under spin echo the qubit stays coherent for τm=1.12 s: about 5 pairs are made in that time
Figure: Hucul et al., Nat. Phys. 11, 37 (2015), arXiv:1403.3696, Fig. 1; ηlink after Covey, Weinfurter and Bernien, npj Quantum Inf. 9, 90 (2023), arXiv:2304.02088
2.6-3

A cavity node already works at C₁ ≈ 2

C1=g22κγ=1.422×0.05×11.2≈2
  • A 40Ca+ ion sits in a 2 cm cavity at 854 nm, finesse 77 000
  • (g,κ,γ)=2π×(1.4, 0.05, 11.2) MHz; C1 is calculated from these
  • By vacuum STIRAP, Ω1 takes the ion from S to D with an H photon, Ω2 to D′ with V
  • The ion and the photon's polarisation end entangled; the fields set α and φ
  • Ion-photon F = 97.4(2) %, post-selected on a detected photon
Stute et al., Nature 485, 482 (2012), arXiv:1301.0275, Fig. 1b; drawing after Fig. 1b
2.6-4

The mirror losses, not the coupling, cost the photons

κoutκ=T1T1+T2+ℓ≈0.16
  • The output mirror transmits T1 = 13 ppm, the other T2 = 1.3 ppm
  • The two mirrors lose ℓ = 68 ppm between them
  • So a photon leaves through the output mirror with probability κout/κ, only 16 % (a)
  • The detectors register 40 % of those: 6.4 % of the cavity photons (b)
  • In the experiment a photon is detected in 5.7 % of the sequences, 40.5 events a second
Stute et al., Nature 485, 482 (2012), arXiv:1301.0275; κout/κ as in Reiserer and Rempe, Rev. Mod. Phys. 87, 1379 (2015), arXiv:1412.2889, Eq. 13
2.6-5

Mirror coatings close to the ion heat its motion

  • A 40Ca+ ion sits a distance d from each mirror-coated fibre tip of a fibre cavity
  • Its motion gains about 0.6 phonons per ms at 600 µm, and 70 at 250 µm (blue)
  • Before the cavity was fitted, it heated by only 13(3) phonons per second
  • A model with no free parameter, noise from the lossy coatings, gives the green squares
  • A hotter ion is collected less efficiently and read out with more errors
Figure: Teller et al., Phys. Rev. Lett. 126, 230505 (2021), arXiv:2103.13846, Fig. 4; O'Reilly et al., Phys. Rev. Lett. 133, 090802 (2024), arXiv:2404.16167
2.6-6

Conversion to 1550 nm carries the ion's photon 50 km

  • A 40Ca+ ion in a cavity with C1=1.47±0.03 emits its photon at 854 nm
  • Fibre loses about 3 dB/km at 854 nm: 10−15 of the photons would survive 50 km
  • It is converted, 25 % efficiently (box), to 1550 nm, where fibre loses 0.181 dB/km
  • After 50 km the ion-photon F=0.86±0.03, post-selected on a click at D
  • Attempts at 2.2 kHz succeed with probability 5.3×10−4: about one photon a second
Krutyanskiy et al., npj Quantum Inf. 5, 72 (2019), arXiv:1901.06317; fibre losses as in section 2.5
2.6-7

Ion-cavity nodes in two buildings 230 m apart are entangled

WindowHeralded F (%)Rate
1 µs88.0−4.7+2.23.5 min−1
Full58.7−2.1+1.70.49 s−1
  • Two 40Ca+ cavity nodes are joined by 520(2) m of fibre (a, b; levels in c)
  • Only two clicks closer in time than the window herald a pair
  • A narrow window keeps the photons that interfere best: higher F, lower rate
  • The memory of the repeater node of section 2.5 decoheres in a fitted 62 ± 3 ms
Figure: Krutyanskiy et al., Phys. Rev. Lett. 130, 050803 (2023), arXiv:2208.14907, Fig. 1, satellite image Google Earth, Landsat / Copernicus; Krutyanskiy et al., Phys. Rev. Lett. 130, 213601 (2023), arXiv:2210.05418
2.6-8

Since 2007 heralded ion links gained in rate and fidelity

  • Each point is a heralded link between two ions, with its fidelity
  • Two traps 2 m apart, linked through lenses, reached 182 pairs a second at 94.0(5) % in 2020
  • The 9.7 s−1 link of 2025 also teleported a CZ gate, deterministically, at 86.2(9) %
  • In 2025 heralded fidelities reached 96.89(8) % at 9.7 s−1 and 97.0(4) % at 0.35 s−1
  • Two ions in one trap gave 79(3) s−1, and 250(8) s−1 with a third ion cooling them (open circle)
Stephenson et al., Phys. Rev. Lett. 124, 110501 (2020), arXiv:1911.10841; O'Reilly et al., Phys. Rev. Lett. 133, 090802 (2024), arXiv:2404.16167; Main et al., Nature 638, 383 (2025), arXiv:2407.00835; Saha et al., Nat. Commun. 16, 2533 (2025), arXiv:2406.01761; earlier points as on the slides before
2.6-9

A time-bin qubit sits in the photon's arrival time

  • The photon is in an early pulse |e⟩, a late one |l⟩ a time τ later, or both (a)
  • Birefringence turns both pulses' polarisation (arrows) alike, and leaves the qubit
  • Two excitations with a 1762 nm π pulse between tie each pulse to one ion state
  • An arm longer by τ overlaps the pulses, and D+, D− measure |e⟩±|l⟩ (b)
  • Between two ions, one early and one late click herald |Ψ±⟩, with no such arm
Saha et al., Nat. Commun. 16, 2533 (2025), arXiv:2406.01761, Eqs. 2 and 3; Knaut et al., Nature 629, 573 (2024), arXiv:2310.01316, Fig. 1a

Neutral atoms

What a computer asks of its link · six ways to bring an atom's photon into a fibre, from a lens to a nanofibre cavity · where they stand · arrays and ensembles

Figure: Fig. 1a of Kato and Aoki, PRL 115, 093603 (2015), arXiv:1505.06774; Đorđević, Science 373, 1511 (2021), arXiv:2105.06485; Goban, PRL 115, 063601 (2015), arXiv:1503.04503; Tiecke, Nature 508, 241 (2014), arXiv:1404.5615; Zhou, PRL 130, 103601 (2023), arXiv:2111.01119; Menon, Nat. 2.7

Cavities give one neutral atom a C₁ from about 1 to 50

C₁ as in Reiserer and Rempe, Rev. Mod. Phys. 87, 1379 (2015), arXiv:1412.2889, Eq. 4; each value from the paper named in its row, Ozawa 2026 a preprint
2.7-1

A surface code corrects errors that stay below its threshold

PL~(pb/pbth)d/2+(ps/psth)d/2
  • A patch of d×d data qubits (open circles) holds one logical qubit
  • Check qubits (dots) measure the parity of four neighbours; a bit flip (×) changes two
  • It fails only if errors chain across it, so its logical error PL falls with the distance d (b)
  • pb and ps are the errors of the local gates and of the seam's Bell pairs (pink)
Sinclair et al., Phys. Rev. Research 7, 013313 (2025), arXiv:2408.08955, Eq. 1; Ramette et al., npj Quantum Inf. 10, 58 (2024), arXiv:2302.01296, Fig. 1b and Eq. 7; curves calculated from the equation
2.7-2

Error correction tolerates noisy pairs but consumes many

  • The seam tolerates about 10 % Bell-pair error at 1 % local error (green, grey; calculated)
  • A distance-20 surface code consumes 40 pairs per cycle and 800 per logical gate
  • 86 pairs at 1 % error, checked as a small code, give one logical pair below 10−10 (calculated)
  • Designs project about 106 pairs per second with one cavity, 5×107 with 30 (orange)
  • Links measured between two atoms (blue) give one pair per 19 s to 208 s
Ramette, npj Quantum Inf. 10, 58 (2024), arXiv:2302.01296; Sinclair, Phys. Rev. Research 7, 013313 (2025), arXiv:2408.08955; Sunami, PRX Quantum 7, 033014 (2026), arXiv:2511.10729; Li and Thompson, PRX Quantum 5, 020363 (2024), arXiv:2401.04075; Hofmann, Science 337, 72 (2012); van Leent, Nature 607, 69 (2022), arXiv:2111.15526
2.7-3

Six ways to bring the photon of an atom into a fibre

  • In A to D the atom sits in free space: in a lens's focus, or between mirrors or fibre tips
  • In E and F it sits in the evanescent field, a few hundred nanometres from glass
van Leent, Nature 607, 69 (2022), arXiv:2111.15526; Hartung, Science 385, 179 (2024), arXiv:2407.09109; Shaw, Nature 650, 320 (2026), arXiv:2506.10919; Grinkemeyer, Science 387, 1301 (2025), arXiv:2410.10787; Đorđević, Science 373, 1511 (2021), arXiv:2105.06485; Kato and Aoki, PRL 115, 093603 (2015), arXiv:1505.06774
2.7-4

Without a cavity, two atoms are entangled once per 106 s

P=η1η22,R=fPd
  • Each atom, in a dipole trap (top left), emits a photon entangled with it (bottom)
  • One excitation gives a click with probability η1=0.9×10−3 or η2=1.25×10−3
  • Success per attempt: P=0.56×10−6, calculated [the paper's 0.54×10−6]
  • Attempts at f = 50 kHz, with both traps loaded a fraction d = 0.35, give the rate R
  • The two Bell states detected have heralded fidelities 0.811 and 0.815 (± 0.028)
Hofmann et al., Science 337, 72 (2012); the trap: Grimm, Weidemüller and Ovchinnikov, Adv. At. Mol. Opt. Phys. 42, 95 (2000), arXiv:physics/9902072, Eq. 12
2.7-5

With conversion, two atoms link over 33 km of fibre

  • The photons are converted in frequency at 57 % efficiency and sent into the fibre
  • The success probability is 3.66×10−6 at 6 km and 1.22×10−6 at 33 km
  • With the reloading of the atoms, that is one heralded event per 19 s and per 208 s
  • The heralded fidelity is at least 0.830(10) at 6 km and 0.622(15) at 33 km
  • Each atom's memory lasts T2≈330 µs, far less than the time between pairs
van Leent et al., Nature 607, 69 (2022), arXiv:2111.15526
2.7-6

Ytterbium at 1389 nm reaches fibre without conversion

  • In ¹⁷¹Yb, ³D₁ decays to ³P₀ at 1389 nm in a fraction 0.64(1) of its decays (calculated)
  • The atom-photon fidelity is 0.90(1), or 0.950(9) corrected, on the photons detected
  • About 0.5 % of the photons reach the fibre, and the rate is below 1 Hz
  • Five atoms feed five fibres; their crosstalk, −13.7(4) dB, is at the noise floor
  • A proposed cavity would give C1=1.3 [the paper's 2.6], a design value
Li et al., Nat. Phys. 21, 1826 (2025), arXiv:2502.17406; the branching ratio: Beloy et al., Phys. Rev. A 86, 051404(R) (2012), arXiv:1208.0552, calculated
2.7-7

One atom in a cavity stores a photon's polarisation

  • Lowering the control field ΩC as the photon arrives stores it; raising it again emits it
  • A σ+ or σ− photon ends in mF=+1 or −1 of F=2: the polarisation is stored
  • Writing, storing and reading succeed in (9.3 ± 1) % at C1≈1.7, calculated
  • The fidelity is 92.7(2) % after 2 µs, on the retrieved photons, not heralded
  • It beats the bounds of 2/3 for single photons and 80 % for these weak pulses, n¯<1
Boozer et al., Phys. Rev. Lett. 98, 193601 (2007), arXiv:quant-ph/0702248; Specht et al., Nature 473, 190 (2011), arXiv:1103.1528
2.7-8

Two single-atom nodes 21 m apart share entanglement

  • Atom A emits a photon into 60 m of fibre, and atom B absorbs it by the reverse process
  • State transfer reaches 84(1) % fidelity at 0.2 % success, post-selected
  • Entanglement reaches a fidelity of 85(1.3) % at 2 % success, not heralded
  • Kept to the earliest photons, the fidelity is 98.7(2.2) %, post-selected
  • 100 µs after its creation the entangled state still has a fidelity of 56(3) %
Figure: Ritter et al., Nature 484, 195 (2012), arXiv:1202.5955, Fig. 1; the transfer: Cirac, Zoller, Kimble and Mabuchi, Phys. Rev. Lett. 78, 3221 (1997), arXiv:quant-ph/9611017
2.7-9

Six atoms in one cavity yield a photon in 88.6 % of attempts

P=1−∏i=1N(1−ηi)
  • The cavity has C1≈1.7, calculated, as for the polarisation memory
  • Up to six atoms sit in a row across the mode, 5.5 µm apart, addressed in turn
  • With one atom, the atom-photon fidelity is 86.6(5) % on the photons detected
  • One atom gives a detected photon in η=33.2(2) % of attempts
  • An attempt fails only if all N atoms fail; with six, P = 88.6(1) % of attempts succeed
Hartung et al., Science 385, 179 (2024), arXiv:2407.09109
2.7-10

A 1.67 mm cavity couples 16 atoms at once (preprint)

  • Tweezers from above place a chain of atoms in the mode of the two mirrors (b, c)
  • One atom has C1 = 56.2(1.7) [the paper's 4g2/(κΓ) = 112.3 ± 3.3]
  • Sixteen atoms at the antinodes keep a mean C1 of 47.9(5) [95.7 ± 0.9]
  • The finesse is 9.5×104, and an objective of NA 0.65 looks in from the side
  • A near-concentric cavity, spaced near twice its mirror radius, gave C1 = 0.084(4)
  • A 1480 nm design for 100 to 200 171Yb atoms reaches 16 in the paper's form
Figure: Ye et al., arXiv:2607.04090 (2026), preprint, Fig. 1b and 1c; Nguyen et al., Phys. Rev. A 96, 031802(R) (2017), arXiv:1706.01256; Huie et al., Phys. Rev. Research 3, 043154 (2021), arXiv:2107.04477, design
2.7-11

Lenses inside a cavity focus its mode far from every surface

  • A curved mirror and a lens, mm to cm away, focus the mode below a micron
  • The finesse is only 40, so the light passes the atom about ten times
  • From the vacuum Rabi splitting of one atom, C1 = 0.8(1) [the paper's 4g2/(κΓ) = 1.6(2)]
  • Each atom gets its own mode (a); 21 are read at once (b), uncorrelated (c)
  • There C1≈0.8 [1.6(2)] is calculated from finesse and waist, not measured on atoms
  • A later array, without atoms, has 603 cavities of mean finesse 114(17)
Figure: Shaw et al., Nature 650, 320 (2026), arXiv:2506.10919, Fig. 1; Shadmany et al., Sci. Adv. 11, eads8171 (2025); Soper et al., Phys. Rev. X 16, 041009 (2026), arXiv:2602.06587
2.7-12

A fibre cavity at C₁ = 51 detects errors in two-atom gates

|D0⟩=(|eg,0⟩−|ge,0⟩)/2
  • In the dark state |D0⟩ the atoms are out of phase: their light into the cavity cancels
  • A strong drive takes |10⟩ round through |D0⟩ with a phase π; |11⟩ is blocked
  • A weak drive empties |10⟩, carving a Bell state: 91(4) % at 32(1) % success, heralded
  • The gate alone reaches 52.5(18) %, deterministic
  • Detecting the errors raises it to 76(2) % at 69(1) % success, heralded
Figure: Grinkemeyer et al., Science 387, 1301 (2025), arXiv:2410.10787, Figs. 1A, 3A and 4A
2.7-13

One guided mode collects a large share of an atom's light

  • Beside a nanofibre, β≈0.13, calculated
  • Γ1D is the decay into the guided mode, Γ′ all other decay
  • At the alligator waveguide (right), Γ1D/Γ′=0.32±0.08: β=0.24
  • Atoms trapped in it reach Γ1D/Γ=1.1±0.1, so β≈0.5
  • An atom at a photonic-crystal cavity (left) has C1=3.9 [the paper's 7.7±0.3]
  • There atom and light shift each other's phase by about π, post-selected
Figures: Tiecke et al., Nature 508, 241 (2014), arXiv:1404.5615, Fig. 1a (left); Goban et al., Phys. Rev. Lett. 115, 063601 (2015), arXiv:1503.04503, Fig. 1(a) (right); Solano et al., Nat. Commun. 8, 1857 (2017), arXiv:1704.07486; Goban et al., Nat. Commun. 5, 3808 (2014), arXiv:1312.3446
2.7-14

Two atoms in one detuned cavity exchange an excitation

J=g2Δac
  • The cavity is detuned by Δac from both atoms, and each couples to it with g (a)
  • For Δac≫g the cavity is hardly ever excited: its photon is only virtual
  • It couples |eg⟩, atom 1 excited, and |ge⟩, atom 2 excited, with the strength J
  • (b) Uncoupled, the energies cross (dashed); coupled, they repel by 2J
Calculated with J/2π=25 MHz, the value of Samutpraphoot et al., Phys. Rev. Lett. 124, 063602 (2020), arXiv:1909.09108
2.7-15

Two atoms at a nanophotonic cavity show the splitting 2J

  • In each map the probe detuning runs across, the two atoms' detuning from each other up
  • One atom at the mode centre has C1=36(2) [the paper's 71(4)], a mean over its motion
  • 1 µm off centre C1=15.5(1.0) [31(2)], so J=2π×25(4) MHz is expected
  • Alone the lines cross (a); together they repel by 2J=2π×50(8) MHz (b), as modelled (c)
Figure: Samutpraphoot et al., Phys. Rev. Lett. 124, 063602 (2020), arXiv:1909.09108, Fig. 4
2.7-16

Two atoms are entangled at a cavity, then one is carried away

  • C1=13.5(5) averaged over the atom's motion, 23.5(5) at rest [the paper's 27(1) and 47(1)]
  • A reflected photon marks the Bell state (carving, next slide): F=0.72(3), post-selected
  • F adds half the populations of |00⟩ and |11⟩ (B) to their coherence, half the parity's swing (C)
  • After one atom is moved 1 µm out in 650 µs: F=0.52(5), post-selected (right)
  • The coherence time T2 is 2.1(1) ms at the cavity and 9.7(8) ms in free space
Figure: Đorđević et al., Science 373, 1511 (2021), arXiv:2105.06485, Figs. 3B, 3C and 4
2.7-17

Carving with two photons succeeds at most half of the time

  • Light leaves by the input mirror at κin and is lost at κsc=κin=κ/2
  • Only |1⟩ couples: with both atoms in |0⟩ the photon is lost, otherwise reflected to D
  • A click removes |00⟩; the flip X⊗X of both atoms turns |11⟩, orange, into |00⟩
  • Two clicks leave (|01⟩+|10⟩)/2, heralded, with probability 1/2
Goswami et al., Phys. Rev. Lett. 136, 050802 (2026), arXiv:2505.02702, Eq. 1; Sørensen and Mølmer, Phys. Rev. Lett. 90, 127903 (2003), arXiv:quant-ph/0206142
2.7-18

One photon passing twice could carve a Bell state every time

  • One photon passes a two-sided cavity twice; both atoms are flipped in between
  • A click at any of the three detectors heralds a Bell state, so success is 1 in principle
Goswami et al., Phys. Rev. Lett. 136, 050802 (2026), arXiv:2505.02702, Eq. 2
2.7-19

The calculated error falls as 1/C₁², so C₁ ≈ 17 gives 0.999

  • Panel a is the error 1−F of the heralded state, panel b the success probability
  • Heralded fidelity 0.999 at the star, C1≈17 [the paper's 4g2/(κγ)≈34], calculated
  • With 2 % loss, κsc=0.02κ, and the input mirror at κ1=0.495κ, success is above 0.9, calculated
  • An error falling as 1/C1 would need C1≈500 [the paper's ~1000] for 0.999
Goswami et al., Phys. Rev. Lett. 136, 050802 (2026), arXiv:2505.02702, Eq. 3, a proposal
2.7-20

A nanofibre between two fibre Bragg gratings is a cavity

  • A fibre Bragg grating's core index steps with the period Λ (inset)
  • Its weak reflections add in phase near λB=2neffΛ, neff the mode's effective index
  • One atom sits beside the nanofibre, in a 33 cm cavity of finesse below 40
  • The atom couples with g0: (g0,κ,γ)/2π=(7.8,6.4,2.6) MHz
  • g0 exceeds κ and γ, so the coupling is strong, at C1=g02/(2κγ)≈1.8
Kato and Aoki, Phys. Rev. Lett. 115, 093603 (2015), arXiv:1505.06774
2.7-21

One Cs atom at a nanofibre cavity reaches C₁ = 2.7

C1=g022κγ=2.7(3)
  • A tweezer holds one Cs atom about 190 nm from a nanofibre between photonic-crystal mirrors
  • C1 is measured [the paper's 4g02/(κγ0)=5.4±0.6, with full widths]
  • Photons seldom arrive in pairs: the pair correlation g(2)(0)≃0.47 is below 1, its value for independent photons
  • From how fast this dip recovers, g0/2π=36±1 MHz; from the photon statistics, 34±2 MHz
  • g0 is below the half width κ/2π=82 MHz: the line does not split, and this is not strong coupling
  • The atom emits 85 ± 2 % of its light into the fibre
Nayak, Wang and Keloth, Phys. Rev. Lett. 123, 213602 (2019), arXiv:1908.03319
2.7-22

171Yb atoms couple to a 1389 nm nanofibre cavity (preprint)

  • Top: 171Yb atoms in tweezers beside a nanofibre between two fibre Bragg gratings
  • Below: spectra of N = 3 to 5 atoms (a); the collective coupling G grows as N (b)
  • g/2π=1.86(17) MHz for one atom, G/2π=3.78(19) MHz for five
  • C1≈2.9 [the paper's Cin=5.6(1.0) counts only the cavity's internal loss]
  • The atoms stay trapped for 6.8(4) s; an entanglement rate of 40 kHz is projected

Nanofibre cavities reach C₁ of 2 to 3; designs project far more

2.8

Colour centres in diamond and quantum dots

A narrow, stable line · nitrogen-vacancy (NV) links and their rates · silicon-vacancy (SiV) centres in nanocavities · the choices side by side · what limits these links · quantum dots

2.8

Symmetry keeps the SiV line narrow in a nanostructure

  • Photons of two emitters interfere only if their lines stay matched (section 2.5)
  • The NV's permanent dipole makes its line follow stray fields (a, blue)
  • The SiV− is inversion symmetric: its shift starts at second order (orange)
  • An electron spin e is the qubit; a nucleus n beside it stores the qubit (b)
  • Each new attempt leaves the electron in a random state and dephases the nucleus
Sipahigil et al., Science 354, 847 (2016), arXiv:1608.05147; Evans et al., Phys. Rev. Applied 5, 044010 (2016), arXiv:1512.03820; Pompili et al., Science 372, 259 (2021), arXiv:2102.04471
2.8-1

A decay from A₂ entangles the NV spin with a photon

R=fPd
  • The NV's ground state is a spin triplet: |0⟩ and |±1⟩ (bottom)
  • Excited to A₂, the centre decays to |+1⟩ or |−1⟩ with σ+ or σ− light
  • The photon's polarisation records the spin state: spin and photon are entangled
  • f is the attempt rate, P the probability of success per attempt, d the duty cycle
  • In the first experiment P=10−6 at f=100kHz: one event every 10 s
Togan et al., Nature 466, 730 (2010), levels after its Fig. 3a
2.8-2

An event-ready herald gave a loophole-free Bell test

  • NV centres in labs 1280 m apart send photons to a beam splitter at C (a)
  • An early and a late click, in different detectors, herald Ψ− (b)
  • The herald is event-ready: it picks the trials before any setting is chosen
  • Each lab chooses its setting and reads its spin before light from the other could arrive
  • The CHSH value S=2.42±0.20 exceeds 2, the local-realist bound (p-value ≤0.039)
  • Heralded at 6.4×10−9 per attempt: fidelity 0.92 ± 0.03, estimated, at least 0.83 ± 0.05
Hensen et al., Nature 526, 682 (2015), arXiv:1508.05949
2.8-3

Two NVs 2 m apart entangle faster than they decohere

ηlink=γent/γdec
  • Each node emits with probability α; one click heralds a pair, F≈1−α
  • Heralded (blue): 0.81(2) at 6 Hz for α=0.05, 0.60(2) at 39 Hz for α=0.3
  • A pair loses its coherence at the rate γdec=5.0(3) Hz (grey line)
  • The link efficiency ηlink, heralded rate γent over γdec, is about 8: 39 Hz over 5 Hz
  • Delivered deterministically at α=0.2 (orange): 0.56(1) at 9.9 Hz
Humphreys et al., Nature 558, 268 (2018), arXiv:1712.07567, Fig. 2d and 4c; Covey, Weinfurter and Bernien, npj Quantum Inf. 9, 90 (2023), arXiv:2304.02088

One SiV makes tunable Raman photons and switches light

  • Only the line from |c⟩ meets the cavity; |u⟩ lies 64 GHz from |c⟩
  • On the left, driven from |u⟩, the SiV emits a Raman photon the laser tunes over 6 GHz
  • It gave about 15 kHz of single photons, g(2)(0)=0.16(3)
  • On the right, one SiV removes 38(3) % of the transmission
  • Single photons scatter and pairs pass: the transmitted light has g(2)(0)=1.50(5)
  • At 4 K phonons mix |u⟩ and |c⟩ in about 10 ns
Figure: Sipahigil et al., Science 354, 847 (2016), arXiv:1608.05147, Fig. 4B and 4C (left), Fig. 3A and 3C (right)
2.8-7

SiV cavities passed C₁ = 1/2, where the reflection flips sign

r=2C1−12C1+1
  • r is the amplitude an overcoupled cavity reflects on resonance, −1 without the SiV
  • r is zero at C1=1/2, the dashed line, and tends to +1 for C1≫1
  • Light markers and brackets give the papers' 4g2/(κγ), which is 2C1
  • From C1≈0.5 [1.0(1)] in 2016, a node reached C1=52±6 [105 ± 11] in 2020
  • The two nodes of the 2024 link had C1=6.2(5) and 0.8(4) [12.4(9) and 1.5(8)]
Reiserer and Rempe, Rev. Mod. Phys. 87, 1379 (2015), arXiv:1412.2889, Eq. 16; Sipahigil et al., Science 354, 847 (2016), arXiv:1608.05147; Bhaskar et al., Nature 580, 60 (2020), arXiv:1909.01323; Knaut et al., Nature 629, 573 (2024), arXiv:2310.01316
2.8-8

A photon reflected off an SiV is entangled with its spin

  • At the probe frequency the cavity reflects only when the spin is up: 94 % against 4 %
  • Flipping the spin between the bins of a time-bin photon leaves (|e↓⟩+|l↑⟩)/2
  • In a, photons of A and B come at any times; the readouts' product m1m2m3 is their parity
  • In b, one photon reflects off two nodes; measured as |±⟩, it heralds Φ±
Bhaskar et al., Nature 580, 60 (2020), arXiv:1909.01323; Knaut et al., Nature 629, 573 (2024), arXiv:2310.01316, Eqs. 1 and 2
2.8-9

An SiV memory node beat direct transmission fourfold

  • To share a key, A and B send photons to an SiV node, C1=52±6 [the paper's 105 ± 11]
  • Its spin holds the first photon until the second arrives: heralded successes at about 0.1 Hz
  • Without a memory the ideal key rate is p/2, with p the channel's transmission
  • With the memory the key rate was 4.1 ± 0.5 times that, over an emulated loss
  • It exceeds 1.44p, the bound for any link without a repeater, with 99.2 % confidence
Figure: Bhaskar et al., Nature 580, 60 (2020), arXiv:1909.01323, Fig. 2a
2.8-10

Two SiV nodes link electrons and store in 29Si nuclei

  • At each node the electron spin meets the photon; a 29Si nucleus is the memory, T2=2.1 s
  • One photon reflected off node A (front), then node B (back), heralds their Bell state
  • The photon is a weak laser pulse with mean photon number μ, well below one
  • At μ=0.017, about 16 mHz, heralded: Φ− reached 0.86(3) and Φ+ 0.74(3)
  • Nucleus pairs came at 6 mHz; the photons were converted to 1350 nm and back, 5.4 % passing
Figure: Knaut et al., Nature 629, 573 (2024), arXiv:2310.01316, Fig. 1, CC BY
2.8-11

Brighter pulses speed up the SiV link and lower its fidelity

  • Average fidelity against heralded rate; the inset shows Φ− and Φ+ at the lowest rate
  • Raising μ (top axis) lifts the rate from 16 mHz to 1.05 Hz, and the fidelity falls
  • The pair stays entangled, above 0.5 (dashed line), up to 1 Hz
  • Over a 35 km loop of deployed fibre: 0.69(7) at 0.23 mHz, heralded, with error detection
  • A photon's state reached an SiV over 50 km of deployed fibre: 87.0 ± 2.5 %, heralded
Figure: Knaut et al., Nature 629, 573 (2024), arXiv:2310.01316, Fig. 2c, CC BY; Bersin et al., PRX Quantum 5, 010303 (2024), arXiv:2307.08619

2.8-14

Quantum dots entangle a spin with the photons they emit

  • On the left, a dot in a micropillar cavity; each photon it emits is entangled with its spin
  • Heralded spin-photon-photon states came at 0.53 MHz at the lens, 0.043 MHz in fibre
  • Spin-photon fidelity ≥ 65 ± 1 %, spin-photon-photon ≥ 59 ± 2 %
  • On the right, a dot in a waveguide: β≈90 %, estimated; it decays 4.2 times faster than in bulk
  • Its spin-photon Bell state reached 76.3(5) %, post-selected, at 1.3 % efficiency end to end
Figures: Coste et al., Nat. Photon. 17, 582 (2023), arXiv:2207.09881, Fig. 1a (left); Meng et al., Nat. Commun. 15, 7774 (2024), arXiv:2310.12038, Fig. 1 (right), CC BY-NC-ND

2.9

Superconducting circuits and transducers

Circuit QED · thermal microwave photons · cold microwave links · four kinds of transducer · rate and added noise · the sideband swap · matching at C = 1 · membranes · piezoelectric nanobeams · electro-optic crystals · Rydberg atoms · the noise map

2.9

A transmon in a resonator reaches strong coupling easily

  • On the left the resonator, an LC circuit, has evenly spaced levels
  • On the right is the transmon, a Josephson junction beside a capacitor
  • Its cosine well spaces the levels unevenly, so a drive at ωq excites |g⟩ to |e⟩ alone
  • Its dipole, about 104ea0, makes g large
  • The resonator's line splits by 2g/2π=350MHz≫κ/2π≈800kHz
Blais et al., Phys. Rev. A 69, 062320 (2004), arXiv:cond-mat/0402216, Table 1; Blais, Grimsmo, Girvin and Wallraff, Rev. Mod. Phys. 93, 025005 (2021), arXiv:2005.12667, Eqs. 22 and 27; Kurpiers et al., Nature 558, 264 (2018), arXiv:1712.08593; Haroche, Brune and Raimond, Nat. Phys. 16, 243 (2020)
2.9-1

A 5 GHz mode at 300 K holds about 1250 thermal photons

nth=1ehf/kBT−1
  • nth is the mean number of thermal photons in a mode of frequency f
  • At 300 K and 5 GHz, nth≈kBT/hf≈1250
  • The circuits run near 10 mK; their photons cannot leave the refrigerator
  • An optical photon at 194 THz has nth≈3×10−14 even at 300 K
  • A transducer moves the quantum state of a microwave photon onto an optical photon
Haroche, Brune and Raimond, Nat. Phys. 16, 243 (2020)
2.9-2

Two processors can be joined by a cold cable or by light

  • (a) A superconducting line below 50 mK carries the microwave photon from qubit Q to qubit Q
  • Between two refrigerators that line runs inside a cryostat of its own
  • The circulator, the circle with the arrow, lets the photon pass one way only
  • (b) A transducer T makes the photon optical, for kilometres of warm fibre (projected)
Blais, Grimsmo, Girvin and Wallraff, Rev. Mod. Phys. 93, 025005 (2021), arXiv:2005.12667, pp. 53 and 54; Magnard et al., Phys. Rev. Lett. 125, 260502 (2020), arXiv:2008.01642; Storz et al., Nature 617, 265 (2023); Delaney et al., Nature 606, 489 (2022), arXiv:2110.09539

2.9-4

Four kinds of transducer join microwave photons to light

  • (a) Electro-optomechanical transducers couple both modes to a membrane's motion
  • (b) Piezo-optomechanical ones turn the field into a 5.2 GHz phonon in a nanobeam
  • (c) In electro-optic ones the field changes the index of LiNbO3, moving light into the next mode
  • (d) Cold 85Rb atoms in a 100 GHz and a 780 nm cavity convert through their Rydberg states
Brubaker et al., Phys. Rev. X 12, 021062 (2022), arXiv:2112.13429; Mirhosseini et al., Nature 588, 599 (2020), arXiv:2004.04838; Sahu et al., Science 380, 718 (2023), arXiv:2301.03315; Kumar et al., Nature 615, 614 (2023), arXiv:2207.10121
2.9-5

A transducer is judged by its photon rate and its added noise

rate=ηt×bandwidth×duty cycle
Nadd=Nout/ηt<1
  • ηt is the efficiency, the fraction of signal photons that leave converted
  • 2 kHz at 50 %, run continuously, equals 20 MHz at 10 % run 6×10−4 of the time
  • The drawing: a beam splitter of transmission ηt, with vacuum entering its unused port
  • Nout is the device's own noise at the output; Nadd refers it to the input, in signal photons
  • Below one added photon a transducer can carry a quantum state
Brubaker et al., Phys. Rev. X 12, 021062 (2022), arXiv:2112.13429; Zeuthen et al., Quantum Sci. Technol. 5, 034009 (2020), arXiv:1610.01099, Fig. 1b
2.9-6

Below one added photon, continuous conversion is fastest

  • Each point is one operating point; the rate is efficiency × bandwidth × duty cycle
  • The grey band is below one added photon, Nadd<1
  • Zhao 2025 ran continuously: 2.2 % over 88.9 ± 2.1 kHz at Nadd=0.94
  • Pulsed devices in the band lose rate to their duty cycle: 0.075 to 5.4 Hz
Zhao et al., Nat. Nanotechnol. 20, 602 (2025), arXiv:2406.02704, Fig. 4d and Table II
2.9-7

Loss alone puts a floor under a transducer's total noise

nin=Nadd+nqnq=1−ηt2ηt
  • nq is the vacuum noise, half a photon, that enters the unused port, referred to the input
  • Each grey line is one total input noise nin; at ηt=10−3 it is at least 500
Blais, Grimsmo, Girvin and Wallraff, Rev. Mod. Phys. 93, 025005 (2021), arXiv:2005.12667, Eq. (92); Caves, Phys. Rev. D 26, 1817 (1982), Eq. (3.30), p. 1825; Brubaker et al., Phys. Rev. X 12, 021062 (2022), arXiv:2112.13429
2.9-8

A pump on a sideband swaps or squeezes light and motion

G=g0ncC=4G2κγm
  • A pump of nc photons raises the single-photon coupling g0 to G
  • A pump at ωc−Ωm, the red sideband, swaps light and motion of frequency Ωm
  • At ωc+Ωm, the blue sideband, it makes photon-phonon pairs: two-mode squeezing
  • The swap is quantum when C exceeds nth; κ and the motion's damping γm are full widths
Dong, Wang and Wang, Natl. Sci. Rev. 2, 510 (2015); Brubaker et al., Phys. Rev. X 12, 021062 (2022), arXiv:2112.13429
2.9-9

Pumps pass a photon from microwave to motion to light

Ce=Γe/γmCo=Γo/γmηt=4CeCo(1+Ce+Co)2
Dong, Wang and Wang, Natl. Sci. Rev. 2, 510 (2015); Brubaker et al., Phys. Rev. X 12, 021062 (2022), arXiv:2112.13429, Eq. 1; Mirhosseini et al., Nature 588, 599 (2020), arXiv:2004.04838; Meesala et al., Nat. Phys. 20, 871 (2024), arXiv:2303.17684
2.9-10

At C = 1 a converter is impedance matched

ηt=4C(1+C)2=8C1(1+2C1)2
  • (a) ηt=1 at C=1 in full widths, or C1=1/2
  • Nothing is reflected there: lecture 1's r=0
  • It is not strong coupling, g≫κ,γ
  • (b) With three modes, ηt peaks at Ce=1+Co
Dong, Wang and Wang, Natl. Sci. Rev. 2, 510 (2015); Brubaker et al., Phys. Rev. X 12, 021062 (2022), arXiv:2112.13429

Membrane transducers cut the added noise to 3.2 photons

Device and settingEfficiencyAdded noise (photons)
Andrews 2014, at 4 K8.6 ± 0.7 %, measuredabout 1500 (Higginbotham 2018)

Andrews et al., Nat. Phys. 10, 321 (2014), arXiv:1310.5276, Fig. 3b; Higginbotham et al., Nat. Phys. 14, 1038 (2018), arXiv:1712.06535, Figs. 2c and 4d; Brubaker et al., Phys. Rev. X 12, 021062 (2022), arXiv:2112.13429
2.9-12

Cooling the membrane sets how low the added noise goes

  • The membrane, pictured between circuit and cavity, has a bath of nth≈1000 phonons
  • The bath damps it at γm; the microwave pump Ce≈1200 times faster (calculated)
  • The pump alone would leave nth/(1+Ce)≈1 phonon
  • The membrane held nm=1.5 phonons, which add 1.0 of the 3.2 added photons
  • Ground-state cooling of the membrane is “necessary and sufficient” for Nadd<1
Figure: Brubaker et al., Phys. Rev. X 12, 021062 (2022), arXiv:2112.13429, Fig. 1a, CC BY 4.0
2.9-13

A membrane transducer read a transmon without harming it

  • The qubit's state shifts its readout cavity, so a reflected microwave pulse carries the state
  • The transducer made that pulse optical; the single-shot readout fidelity was about 0.4
  • The Ramsey fringes give the coherence time T2: 20.7±0.2 µs, laser on; 20.4±0.2 µs, off
  • The microwave pump added (3±1)×10−3 photons to the readout cavity: low back-action
  • The chain transmitted 1.9×10−3 and added 740 photons; the transducer alone added 23
Figure: Delaney et al., Nature 606, 489 (2022), arXiv:2110.09539, Fig. 3a
2.9-14

A nanobeam turned a transmon's excitation into light

  • On this chip a transmon (SC qubit) passed its excitation to a 5.2 GHz phonon
  • A laser pulse made the phonon a 1541.7 nm photon, at ηt=(0.88±0.16)×10−5
  • The added noise was Nadd=0.57±0.2; the readout destroyed the state, at 100 Hz
  • A later device heralded microwave-optical photon pairs at 0.14 Hz, with no qubit
Figure: Mirhosseini et al., Nature 588, 599 (2020), arXiv:2004.04838, Fig. 1e; Meesala et al., Nat. Phys. 20, 871 (2024), arXiv:2303.17684
2.9-15

A pulsed electro-optic converter neared one added photon

  • A modulator (AOM) cuts the pump into 100 or 300 ns pulses at 5 to 2000 Hz for the disk (DUT)
  • From optics to microwave the added noise was Nadd=1.11−0.07+0.15, from measured noise
  • Microwave to optics, 0.16−0.01+0.02 at 8.7 % efficiency, inferred; 0.41±0.02 at up to 15 %
  • At 500 Hz the refrigerator's coldest stage warmed from 7 mK to at most 60 mK
Figure: Sahu et al., Nat. Commun. 13, 1276 (2022), arXiv:2107.08303, Fig. 1, CC BY 4.0
2.9-16

Electro-optic transducers entangled light and drove a qubit

  • (b) A pump photon splits into a microwave and an optical photon
  • The outputs were 0.72−0.25+0.31 dB (2σ) squeezed: deterministic entanglement
  • The fitted cooperativity was C=0.18±0.01 (full widths, 2σ)
  • On a thin-film chip, two laser tones made a microwave tone that drove a transmon
  • It converted ηt=1.18 % over 30 MHz, with under 0.12 noise photons from the light

2.9-17

Cold atoms convert 100 GHz photons into 780 nm light

  • On the left, 85Rb atoms sit where a 100 GHz niobium cavity crosses a 780 nm cavity, at 5 K
  • The internal efficiency is 58(11) %, over a bandwidth of 360(20) kHz
  • The added noise, 0.6 photons, is the thermal occupation of the 100 GHz mode at 5 K
  • End to end the efficiency is about 2.5 %, limited by the weak out-coupling at 100 GHz
  • Rydberg level spacings fall as 1/n3: higher n could reach 10 GHz transmons (proposed)
Figure: Kumar et al., Nature 615, 614 (2023), arXiv:2207.10121, Fig. 1a and 1c; Saffman, Walker and Mølmer, Rev. Mod. Phys. 82, 2313 (2010), arXiv:0909.4777, Eq. 6
2.9-18

Four fields close a loop through two Rydberg states

𝐤297+𝐤mm=𝐤780+𝐤481
  • A 297 nm laser drives 5S1/2 to 35P1/2, detuned by Δ
  • A 100 GHz photon from the cavity completes the step to 36S1/2
  • A 481 nm laser takes the atom to 5P3/2, which emits 780 nm light into the cavity
  • The emission is collective only when the four wave vectors close the loop
  • The efficiency peaks near Δ/2π≈4 MHz, where the conversion is matched
Kumar et al., Nature 615, 614 (2023), arXiv:2207.10121, Fig. 1a, Fig. 3a and Methods
2.9-19

Heat and noise from the pumps limit today's transducers

  • Pump light breaks Cooper pairs: a transmon took about 8 ms to recover
  • A 154 mW pulse (plot) raised the microwave bath from 0.03 ± 0.01 to 0.09 ± 0.03 photons
  • A strong microwave pump makes the circuit itself emit noise
  • Cables and circulators between transducer and qubit lost 46 % of the signal
  • The target for a converter is over 50 % efficiency at a signal-to-noise ratio over 100
  • A heralded pair source keeps its fidelity when photons are lost
Figure: Sahu et al., Science 380, 718 (2023), arXiv:2301.03315, Fig. 2D; Delaney et al., Nature 606, 489 (2022), arXiv:2110.09539; Warner et al., Nat. 2.10-2

Link rates fall by orders of magnitude over distance

R=fPd,P=η2/2
  • The rate is the attempt rate f times the probability per attempt P times the duty cycle d
  • With a two-photon herald P=η2/2, so every loss on the way, fibre included, enters squared
  • Yu 2020 is not plotted, since its 1.5 Hz at 50 km is an estimate
  • The rate of van Leent 2022 is averaged over the run, reloading included
Data: the papers of the two tables before; P=η2/2: Krutyanskiy et al., npj Quantum Inf. 5, 72 (2019), arXiv:1901.06317
2.10-3

Linked error-corrected modules tolerate per-cent pair errors

  • Local CZ gates reach 99.93 % in superconducting circuits and 99.5 % in tweezer arrays
  • Error correction works up to a pair error of 8.8 % at 1.1 % local error, about 10 % at about 1 %
  • A preprint finds about 13 % at a local error of 0.1 %
  • Only one measured remote pair is below them: 96.89(8) %, heralded, at 9.7 s−1 over 2 m
Blais, Rev. Mod. Phys. 93, 025005 (2021), arXiv:2005.12667; Evered, Nature 622, 268 (2023), arXiv:2304.05420; Sinclair, Phys. Rev. Research 7, 013313 (2025), arXiv:2408.08955; Ramette, npj Quantum Inf. 10, 58 (2024), arXiv:2302.01296; Liu, arXiv:2603.06513 (2026); Main, Nature 638, 383 (2025), arXiv:2407.00835
2.10-4

Each transition of ytterbium serves a different task

  • The broad 399 nm line loads the atoms, the narrow 556 nm line cools them
  • The metastable ³P₀ and ³P₂ states hold the memory
  • The 1389, 1480 and 1539 nm lines, from ³P up to ³D, lie in the telecom band
  • The ground state ¹S₀ of ¹⁷¹Yb has two nuclear-spin sublevels, split only by a field
Takasu, Phys. Rev. Lett. 93, 123202 (2004); Xu, Phys. Rev. Lett. 113, 033003 (2014), arXiv:1406.2340; Porsev and Derevianko, Phys. Rev. A 69, 042506 (2004), arXiv:physics/0312006; Beloy, Phys. Rev. A 86, 051404(R) (2012), arXiv:1208.0552; Li, Nat. Phys. 21, 1826 (2025), arXiv:2502.17406; Huie, Phys. Rev. Research 3, 043154 (2021), arXiv:2107.04477; NIST ASD
2.10-5

A linewidth is the sum of the partial decay rates

Γ=∑jΓj,bj=Γj/Γ
  • ³D₁ has a lifetime τ = 329.3 ± 7.1 ns, so its linewidth is Γ/2π = 483(10) kHz
  • A calculated branching ratio b = 0.64(1) gives a partial rate into ³P₀ of 309(8) kHz
  • The 1389 nm line is therefore 483 kHz wide, not 309 kHz
  • C1 takes γ=Γ/2 of the full width; a fraction b of the decays ends in ³P₀
  • A nanofibre pulled in an H₂–O₂ flame loses 8 % at 1389 nm, in a D₂–O₂ flame under 1 %
Beloy et al., Phys. Rev. A 86, 051404(R) (2012), arXiv:1208.0552 (lifetime, b); Li et al., Nat. Phys. 21, 1826 (2025), arXiv:2502.17406 (branching); Horikawa et al., Opt. Lett. 50, 5294 (2025), arXiv:2506.06123 (OH absorption)
2.10-6

On a nanofibre, one stored photon needs thousands of atoms

β=Γ1DΓ1D+Γ′,C1=Γ1D2Γ′
1−ηmem≈5.8/OD,OD≈2Nβ
  • The atom emits into the guided mode at Γ1D and into all other modes at Γ′
  • The lab's design value Γ1D/Γ′ = 0.05 gives C1 = 0.025 and β≈0.048
  • Measured nanofibres give β=OD/2N of 0.3 to 2 % for N atoms
  • At 0.05, a storage error 1−ηmem of 1 % needs about 6000 atoms
Gorshkov et al., Phys. Rev. A 76, 033805 (2007), arXiv:quant-ph/0612083; Vetsch et al., Phys. Rev. Lett. 104, 203603 (2010), arXiv:0912.1179; Han et al., arXiv:2509.22958 (2025), preprint; Pache et al., Phys. Rev. A 112, L011701 (2025), arXiv:2407.02278; Asenjo-Garcia et al., Phys. Rev. X 7, 031024 (2017), arXiv:1703.03382, Fig. 18
2.10-7

The cavity architectures reach C₁ from about 2 to 50

  • A fibre Fabry-Pérot cavity: C₁ = 50.5(1.0) [101(2)]
  • A photonic-crystal cavity: 13.5(5) [27(1)], a mean over the thermal motion of the atom
  • Nanofibre cavities: about 1.8, measured, and about 2.9 [internal 5.6(1.0)], preprint
  • A nanofibre-cavity design: an internal 90, projected
  • In brackets, each paper's value: 4g2/(κγ) with full widths, or internal (cavity loss only)
The lab's nanofibre cavity: picture to come

2.10-8

The IAMS lab puts ytterbium in tweezers beside a nanofibre

  • Tweezers take ¹⁷¹Yb atoms, drawn as clocks, to chosen places in the nanofibre's evanescent field
  • The memory is ³P₀; the photon, at 1389 nm in the telecom band, leaves through the fibre

What limits each platform today, in its own papers

PlatformWhat limits itMeasured
Trapped ionsPhotons detected per attempt; recoolingA photon detected in 2.3(1) % of attempts (O'Reilly 2024); 2.254 ms of recooling per 200 µs of attempts, 9.7 s−1 (Main 2025)
Neutral atomsCollection without a cavity; a surface near the atomAbout 0.5 % of the light reaches the fibre through a lens (Li 2025); at a chip cavity, heating of unknown source and 0.5 pairs per minute (Đorđević 2021); on a nanofibre, a trap lifetime of 52 ± 5 ms (Nayak 2019)
Colour centresPhoton detection, conversion, coolingNV: photon detection efficiency about 4×10−4 (Humphreys 2018); SiV: two conversions pass 5.4 %, nodes below 200 mK (Knaut 2024)
Quantum dotsLoss after the dot; the spin against the heraldHeralded states at 0.53 MHz at the lens, 0.043 MHz in fibre (Coste 2023); 1.3 % end to end (Meng 2024); spins read out before the herald arrived (Stockill 2017)
Circuits and transducersPump heat and noise; loss before the qubitA qubit recovered from the light in about 8 ms (Mirhosseini 2020); a 154 mW pulse raised the microwave bath from 0.03 to 0.09 photons (Sahu 2023); 46 % lost before the qubit (Warner 2025)
Atomic ensemblesMemory time against the time to heraldMemories of about 70 µs, 50 km of fibre (Yu 2020); heralded at 1.93 Hz, 0.672(32) post-selected on a photon from each memory, read after 5 µs (Liu 2024)
